explain.say: New Year at Camelot. The feast is loud, until a giant knight rides in, green from head to toe, even his horse. He offers a game: strike me with this axe, and in a year and a day I strike you back. An unknown poet wrote this in the late 1300s. Follow Gawain's panels.

explain.say: On his journey Gawain stays with Lord Bertilak, who proposes an exchange: what I win hunting, you get; what you win indoors, I get. Look at the sort. Each day a hunt outside matches a temptation in Gawain's bedroom. On day three, like the sly fox, he hides the girdle. Why the fox on the third day?

explain.say: At the Green Chapel the axe falls three times. Two feints, then a small nick, for the girdle he hid. Then the twist on the board: the Green Knight is Bertilak, sent by Morgan le Fay to test Camelot. Did Gawain pass or fail?

explain.say: The last panel. Gawain is ashamed and wears the girdle as a sign of his fault, but Camelot laughs kindly and all wear green sashes. His shield's pentangle stood for perfect truth; the girdle admits human weakness. Excellent. Challenge: argue whether Gawain failed, or proved human.

faq.a: The Green Knight's challenge: anyone may strike him one blow with his axe if they agree to receive a return blow a year and a day later. Gawain accepts and beheads him.
asks: What is the challenge in Sir Gawain?

faq.q: What is the exchange of winnings?
faq.a: Bertilak's bargain: each day he gives Gawain what he wins hunting, and Gawain gives him whatever he gains at the castle. Gawain hands over the kisses but hides the girdle.
asks: What deal does Gawain make with Bertilak?

faq.q: Why does Gawain keep the green girdle?
faq.a: The lady says it will protect the wearer from death. Facing the axe, Gawain keeps it to save his life, breaking his promise to hand over everything he receives.
asks: Why does Gawain hide the girdle?

faq.q: Who is the Green Knight really?
faq.a: Lord Bertilak de Hautdesert, transformed by Morgan le Fay, who sent him to test the pride of Arthur's court and frighten Guinevere.
The five-pointed star on Gawain's shield stands for perfect truth: five sets of five virtues and senses, linked endlessly. The girdle later shows he is not perfect.

facts: The poem survives in one manuscript, Cotton Nero A.x, with Pearl, Cleanness and Patience.
It has 2,530 lines in 101 stanzas, each ending with a short rhyming bob and wheel.
J. R. R. Tolkien and E. V. Gordon published an edition in 1925.
